dorobot-nexus · UX Design Spec · v1

The simulator is the window

A native training studio that ports zealot into a single binary — reinforcement learning for humanoids where the thing that simulates and the thing that renders are the same process, on the same GPU. Not a dashboard bolted onto a headless job. A console you can reach into.

Product standalone, sibling to DoRobot Studio Ports zealot on nexus Built from DoRobot Studio's widget set Robot Unitree G1 · 29 DOF Surfaces 6
01

A sibling, not a tab

scope

dorobot-nexus shares DoRobot Studio's widgets and visual language, and shares nothing else. They are two products because they have two operators.

DoRobot Studiodorobot-nexus
Operatorruns the robottrains the policy
Session lengthminutes, hands on hardwarehours, hands off
Loopseconds — record, review, savetens of minutes — launch, judge, kill
Scarce resourcehuman attentioncompute, and patience
The documenta dataseta run
Failure feels likea bad takea plateau you noticed too late

Merging them produces an application whose navigation is half irrelevant at any given moment. Keeping them apart costs one thing — a shared widget crate — and that crate already exists.

What is shared

makepad-app-shell (panel grid, drag, persistence), RobotView, TimeSeriesPlot, Timeline, VideoPlayer, EpisodeList, and the ux token family. Every surface below is assembled from widgets already running in this workspace. The accent shifts from blue to violet — the only visual signal that you are in the simulator and not on the floor.

02

One process, one GPU

the thesis

Every RL trainer in production today is a headless process plus a browser tab. That split is not a design choice — it is a consequence of the trainer being Python and the viewer being something else.

nexus runs its physics on wgpu. Makepad renders on the GPU. There is no reason for them to be different processes, and once they are not, four things become possible that a dashboard cannot offer at any price:

  • Single-step. Advance the simulation one tick and read the observation vector that produced the action. The policy stops being a black box the moment you can halt it between frames.
  • Perturb. Push the robot mid-rollout and watch the recovery. Robustness stops being a number in a table and becomes something you did with your hand.
  • Scrub without latency. The state is in memory, not behind a socket, so a rollout scrubs like video.
  • Probe while training. Open a checkpoint in Inspect while the run continues in the background, on the same device, without checkpointing to disk first.

This is the whole product claim. Everything else is careful arrangement of things that already exist.

02b

The body

unitree g1

The design targets the Unitree G1, 29 degrees of freedom — the body zealot already trains whole-body control against, which makes it the one robot where the simulation half of this product has something to say on day one.

The model is g1_29dof_rev_1_0.urdf from Unitree's unitree_ros, BSD-3-Clause. It is in this repository and it renders today in makepad-urdf-player with no loader changes: 39 links, 35 carrying meshes, 29 movable joints. Not a claim — a screenshot, taken before this document was written.

Two practical notes that shaped the import design below. Upstream ships 167 meshes totalling 110 MB covering every G1 variant including dexterous hands; this URDF references 35 of them, 20 MB, so the meshes are fetched from the URDF's own reference list rather than committed. And the G1 uses the same relative mesh convention the SO-100 already did, which is why nothing in the loader had to change — a coincidence the import flow cannot assume in general.

03

What the operator is actually doing

the job

For the hours a run takes, the operator asks three questions in strict order. Each screen exists to answer one of them, and the order is why the navigation is arranged as it is.

Q1
Is it learning?
Reward rising, falls falling, throughput holding. Answered by Train in ten minutes.
Q2
Is it learning the right thing?
Per-term curves, the environment grid, and the diagnosis rail. Answered by Train and Inspect.
Q3
Will it transfer?
Cross-simulator agreement and behaviour at the edges of the randomization. Answered by Validate.

Q1 is cheap and most tools answer it. Q2 is where hours are lost and almost nothing answers it. Q3 is where projects fail, months later, on real hardware.

04

Six laws

held to
LAW 01

The run is the document

Every artifact — checkpoint, curve, validation, export — hangs off a run. There is no loose file anywhere in this product, because the checkpoint graveyard is the natural end state of every training tool that lacks this.

LAW 02

Name every term

A reward is a list of named, weighted terms — never an anonymous scalar. Naming is not documentation here; it is what makes per-term curves, per-term regressions and per-term blame possible at all.

LAW 03

Diagnose, don't display

Showing a curve is table stakes. The product watches the metrics for known failure signatures and names them in words — reward hacking, dead signal, physics overfit — with what to try next.

LAW 04

Long work is abandonable

Progress is reported in env-steps, not spinners. Any run stops, resumes and compares against its siblings. A six-hour job you cannot judge at minute ten is a six-hour job you will not stop.

LAW 05

Provenance travels

A checkpoint carries its scene, reward weights, seed, commit and validation record. Exported artifacts carry it too. A policy you cannot trace is a policy you cannot ship.

LAW 06

One panel vocabulary

Inherited from DoRobot Studio unchanged. A reward curve, a joint trace and a robustness sweep are one widget with different series. Learn the console once.

05

The six surfaces

design intent

Runs

home

Answer "what have I trained, what is running, and which one was actually good?" — and make comparing two runs a first-class act rather than a spreadsheet.

Kills

A directory of timestamped folders, and the question "which config produced ckpt_00420.pt?" that nobody can answer a week later.

Anatomy

  • Run card — thumbnail from the final rollout, monospace name, scene and seed, a reward sparkline, and status chips: training, trained, validated, failed.
  • Compare — select two or more; per-term curves overlay and the config difference is highlighted field by field. This is how "why was Tuesday's run better" stops being folklore.
  • Queue and GPU rail — what is running, what is next, and whether the device is saturated.
  • Export — checkpoint to Hugging Face or ONNX with the provenance manifest attached (Law 05).

Built from

EpisodeList becomes the run tree; the card grid is the Library card component with a different noun; sparklines are TimeSeriesPlot in miniature.

Scene

authoring

Define the world and the body: robot, terrain, randomization, and the observation/action contract — and see it before spending GPU-hours in it.

Kills

Editing a config struct, launching, and discovering twenty minutes later that friction randomization was never enabled.

Anatomy

  • Viewport — the live nexus scene, orbitable, with the robot at rest pose on the selected terrain.
  • Terrain tiles — flat, slope, stairs, rough, each carrying the curriculum thresholds that promote between them.
  • Randomization ranges — mass, friction, latency, motor strength, as two-handled sliders with a resample action that redraws the viewport from a fresh draw. Domain randomization becomes something you looked at rather than something you declared.
  • Observation / action contract — an explicit table of what the policy sees and emits, with shapes. This is the document sim-to-real arguments are settled with.

Adding a robot

A robot is a reusable artifact, not a property of one scene, so Scene's robot slot opens a picker over a robot library — and a robot enters that library through an import that is a validation report, not a file dialog.

That distinction is the whole design. Importing a URDF fails silently in a small number of predictable ways, and every one of them costs an afternoon: a mesh path that does not resolve, a package:// URI that assumes a ROS workspace, joints with no limits, links with zero inertia that make the solver explode, millimetres where the file claims metres, or no collision geometry at all. A file picker reports none of these. A report reports all of them, before the robot is accepted.

  • Resolve every mesh by name — the single most common import failure, and the one a generic "failed to load" message wastes the most time on.
  • Structural checks — URDF parses, kinematic tree is a tree, joint limits present, inertia non-zero, collision geometry present, units plausible. Each is pass, warn or fail rather than a single verdict, because a robot with no collision geometry is renderable but not simulable.
  • Render before accepting — the rest pose in the viewport is the check no static analysis replaces. A robot assembled inside-out parses perfectly.
  • Tag joint groups — upper body, lower body, hands. Whole-body work needs to know which joints belong to which half, and the import is the only moment someone knows.
  • Fetch what is missing — a robot may declare a mesh source, so an import with unresolved meshes can offer to fetch them rather than simply refusing.

Built from

RobotView for the viewport — the same widget that renders the calibration mirror in Studio. Panels and drag layout from makepad-app-shell.

Task

reward authoring

Say what "good" means, in terms that can be blamed individually when the policy games one of them.

Kills

A reward function as a block of arithmetic, where the only observable is the sum — so a term that is being exploited is invisible by construction.

Anatomy

  • Term composer — each row is a named term, a weight slider, and an inline sparkline of that term's contribution in the most recent run. Weights are edited against evidence, not intuition.
  • Curriculum ladder — stages with explicit promotion thresholds; the current stage is highlighted, and a stage that never promotes is the single most common silent stall in RL training.
  • Termination — the conditions that end an episode, as toggles with counts from the last run. A termination that never fires and one that fires constantly are both bugs.
  • Success criterion — the one number the run is judged by, stated before the run rather than chosen afterwards to flatter the result.

Built from

TimeSeriesPlot in sparkline mode per row; the ladder is the Hardware wizard's stepper component with different labels.

Train

flagship

Judge a six-hour run at minute ten, and know why — not merely whether — it is failing.

Kills

TensorBoard in a second window, tail -f in a third, ssh in a fourth, and the fact that none of them can show you the robot.

What only this product can do

The environment grid. A GPU simulator is running thousands of environments already; rendering sixteen of them costs almost nothing, and two robots falling over while the reward curve rises is a diagnosis no scalar metric will ever give you.

Anatomy

  • Run header — envs, steps/s, elapsed, progress in env-steps (Law 04). Throughput is a health signal: a collapse means the loop left the GPU.
  • Per-term reward curves — one line per Task term. Total reward rising while track_lin_vel is flat and feet_air_time soars is reward hacking, visible at a glance.
  • Environment grid — sixteen live envs as a contact sheet, falls tinted red.
  • Diagnosis rail — the app's opinion, in words, from the catalogue in §07 (Law 03).
  • Checkpoint rail — auto-saved, scored, promotable, provenance attached.

Built from

TimeSeriesPlot small-multiples — the component already built for the episode player's per-joint lanes. Grid cells are sixteen small RobotViews fed by a strided readback of env root states.

Inspect

the differentiator

Stop treating the policy as a black box. Drive a checkpoint, halt it between ticks, push it over, and read what it saw.

Kills

Recording a video of a rollout, watching it, and guessing. Also kills the entire practice of writing a bespoke script every time you want to test one perturbation.

What only this product can do

Reach into the simulation. Because the sim is in this process, a push is a function call and the response is on screen in the same frame. Every other tool in this space requires you to write and re-run a script to ask the same question.

Anatomy

  • Viewport with transport — play, pause, single-step, slow motion. The scrubber is the same Timeline widget the episode player uses, so the interaction is already learned.
  • Perturbation — apply an impulse of chosen magnitude and direction. Recovery time and whether it fell are recorded as a probe result attached to the checkpoint.
  • Observation readout — the actual vector the policy consumed on this tick, named per element. An observation that is silently zero is a class of bug otherwise found days later.
  • Torque and contact — per-joint effort bars and foot pressure. Saturated torque explains gaits that look inexplicable from outside.

Built from

RobotView plus Timeline plus TimeSeriesPlot — three widgets already shipping in the episode player, rearranged. This is Law 06 paying for itself.

Validate

the gate

Predict, indoors, whether this policy will survive contact with a real robot.

Kills

Finding out on the floor. Also kills the single-number success rate that hides a policy which works perfectly at the centre of the randomization and nowhere else.

Anatomy

  • Robustness surface — sweep two axes of the randomization (friction × payload, say) and render a pass/fail heatmap. A policy that is green in the middle and red at the edges has not learned the task; it has learned the average. This is the single best sim-to-real predictor the product can compute.
  • Cross-simulator — the same policy in nexus and in MuJoCo, side by side, with divergence over time. Zealot already treats MuJoCo as its reference validator; this makes that routine visible.
  • Comparison table — this run against previous runs and against published references, on the metrics the Task screen declared in advance.
  • Probe log — every perturbation tried in Inspect, aggregated. Manual poking accumulates into evidence instead of evaporating.

Built from

The heatmap is the one new draw — a DrawQuad grid with a colour ramp, roughly the size of the drift strip already built for the player's timeline.

07

The diagnosis catalogue

law 03, in detail

The design's strongest claim is that the app should have an opinion. These are the patterns it watches for, the signature it matches, and what it says. Every one is computable from metrics the trainer already emits.

PatternSignatureWhat it usually meansWhat the rail suggests
Reward hackingtotal reward ↑, falls ↑, one term dominatingan exploitable termopen the dominating term in Task; add a penalty or cap
Dead signalreward flat, entropy flat, from step zeroobservation scaling or initcheck the contract table for a zeroed observation
Curriculum stallstage never promotes, reward plateaus below thresholdpromotion gate too strictlower the threshold, or widen the stage's terrain
Physics overfitin-sim ↑, cross-sim ↓a gait exploiting the solverwiden randomization; re-run Validate's sweep
Brittlenessgreen centre, red edges on the robustness surfacerandomization too narrowextend the failing axis in Scene
Throughput collapsesteps/s drops sharply mid-runthe loop left the GPUcheck readback frequency; the env grid is the usual culprit
Torque saturationeffort bars pinned in Inspectmotor limits below task demandthe robot may be under-actuated for this task

None of these are novel insights to an experienced RL engineer — which is the point. They are exactly the knowledge that currently lives in one person's head and is unavailable to everyone else on the team at 2am.

08

The loop

flow
Fork a run from the closest previous one.

Runs are the document; new work starts as a diff against something that already worked, not a blank config.

Adjust one thing in Scene or Task.

The diff is displayed. One change per run is a discipline the UI makes visible rather than merely recommending.

Launch, and judge at minute ten.

Per-term curves plus the environment grid plus the diagnosis rail. Kill it here if it is hacking a term — this is where the hours are saved.

Probe the best checkpoint in Inspect.

Single-step through a stumble, push it sideways, read the observation. Probes attach to the checkpoint as evidence.

Sweep it in Validate.

Robustness surface first, cross-simulator second. Green centre with red edges sends you back to Scene, not to hardware.

Export with provenance.

Scene, weights, seed, commit, probe log and validation record travel with the artifact — into DoRobot Studio's Eval, or anywhere else.

The handoff to DoRobot Studio is a file, not an integration. That is deliberate: the two products meet at an artifact boundary, which is the only coupling that does not rot.

09

Evaluation

nielsen's ten heuristics

Scored against Jakob Nielsen's ten usability heuristics — a standard rubric published in 1994 and not written for this project — rather than against criteria chosen by the author of the design.

9.5/ 10 mean
across ten heuristics
HeuristicScoreHow the design addresses it
1 · Visibility of status10Progress in env-steps, live throughput, sixteen running environments and a per-term breakdown. The system's state is the screen.
2 · System ↔ real world9.5Reward terms carry domain names; the robot is shown as a robot. The vocabulary is the engineer's, not the framework's.
3 · Control and freedom10Every run stops, resumes, forks and compares; single-step and slow motion in Inspect. Law 04 is this heuristic.
4 · Consistency and standards10One panel vocabulary inherited wholesale from DoRobot Studio; the transport in Inspect is literally the episode player's.
5 · Error prevention9Success criterion declared before the run; randomization previewed before launch; export blocked without validation. Weaker on protecting a long run from an accidental config edit.
6 · Recognition over recall10Provenance on every card; the config diff is shown rather than remembered. The checkpoint graveyard is designed out.
7 · Flexibility and efficiency9Fork-from-previous for experts, previews for newcomers. No keyboard-first path is specified yet, which a daily user would want.
8 · Aesthetic and minimalist9Panels carry only diagnostic content. Train is dense by necessity and is the screen most at risk of crowding.
9 · Diagnose and recover10The diagnosis catalogue is the design's centre: named failure modes, matched signatures, suggested actions. Few tools in this category attempt it at all.
10 · Help and documentation8.5Diagnosis text teaches in context, but no reference material or onboarding path is specified. The weakest heuristic here.

What this number is, and is not

The rubric is external; the scoring is still mine. A heuristic evaluation is normally run by three to five independent evaluators precisely because a single evaluator — especially the designer — finds a fraction of the problems and rates the rest generously.

Treat 9.5 as: this design has a defensible answer for each of Nielsen's ten, and two known weak spots (onboarding, keyboard efficiency) that I have not solved. It is not a measured usability score. That requires operators attempting tasks, and no operator has seen this.

The honest risks

  • nexus is young — its own README says "still under heavy development and is still missing many features." The product's foundation may move underneath it.
  • The environment grid's cost is unmeasured. Sixteen viewports onto a live sim is the one component that could contend with training throughput. Fallback: a sampled contact sheet at 2 Hz.
  • In-process training is a strong claim. A trainer that panics takes the UI with it. The mitigation — trainer on its own thread behind a channel, with the option to run out-of-process — should be designed in from the start, not retrofitted after the first crash.
